The cloak hides a macroscopic spherical object from human sight from three orthogonal directions.
The design uses a 3D homogeneous polyhedral transformation to simplify material requirements.
Spatially invariant refractive index discretization replaces anisotropic indices with isotropic indices.
The cloak is made from isotropic optical glasses ZLaF78 (permittivity 3.61) and ZBaF1 (permittivity 2.63).
Water fills the gaps between glass segments in the cloak.
The cubic cloak has a side length of 100 mm.
The hidden object is a steel ball with a diameter of 38 mm.
The compression ratio of the cloak is approximately 0.172.
The cloak operates effectively at visible wavelengths of 532 nm and 650 nm.
The hidden region volume is about 7.6% of the total cloak volume.
The cloak works for fully polarized visible light and is symmetric in three orthogonal directions.
The polyhedral transformation bends light at segment interfaces rather than requiring spatially inhomogeneous materials.
Replacing anisotropic materials with isotropic ones limits the cloak's effectiveness to certain incident directions.
Experimental results show the recovery of image patterns behind the cloak, confirming invisibility.
The cloak is operational under incoherent light illumination.
The approach is inspired by and extends quasi-conformal mapping methods used in carpet cloaks.
The cloak affects transmitted light by transforming a point into an inner sphere, requiring highly anisotropic parameters in theory.
The device is the first large-scale 3D visible-light cloak effective for multiple viewing angles.
The cloak's design and fabrication overcome previous limitations restricting cloaks to 2D or narrow viewing angles.
Potential improvements include more accurate fabrication to reduce image distortion.
